new_statements.quote: In the above examples we can see that stress falls on the first syllable if none of the above factors affects it. We can conclude that stress is predictable in the Ramoaaina language. To predict it we need to make a hierarchy of syllable strength, as follows: strong (C)V1(C) (C)V2C (C)V2 (C)V3C weak (C)V3 In the above hierarchy V1 stands for the vowel [ɐ],V3 for the vowel [ə], and V2 for all other vowels. [...] Stress Assignment rule: Stress is always assigned to the strongest syllable. If syllables have equal strength, stress is assigned to the first one.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Unbounded prominence-driven stress: primary stress goes to the 'strongest' syllable of the word by the scale (C)ɐ(C) > closed full-vowel syllable > open full-vowel syllable > closed schwa syllable > open schwa syllable ([ɐ] = orthographic <aa> attracts stress, [ə] = orthographic <a> repels it); when syllables tie, the leftmost wins, so words of uniform syllable type have initial stress (e.g. [ˈpoŋo], [ˈkuro], [liˈmɐnə], [məˈgo], [teŋˈlik]? no: [ˈteŋlik], [mələˈlər]). The authors' own 1999 OPD compresses this to 'Stress normally falls on the first syllable', with short function words <a> 'the', <aa> 'past' unstressed. Tone and length are stated to be non-phonemic (sec. 2.3).
new_statements.secondary_stress: "Secondary stress falls on every second syllable either way from the syllable which carries the primary stress" (3.1.2, p.5), e.g. [ˌmələˈlər] 'picture', [ˌtenəˈlik] 'his brother', [ˈɐkɐˌkur] 'story'.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with a medial palatalized/labialized voiced consonant take stress on an open schwa syllable instead of the closed one ([ˈnəmʲən] 'sweet', [təˈləŋʷən] 'tired', [ˈtəbʷən] 'woman'), tentatively explained by treating the complex consonant as ambisyllabic; [ˈməge] 'sun' is listed as an unexplained exception (stress on [ə] despite a full vowel). OPD 1999 adds that short function words <a> 'the, a' and <aa> 'past tense' are unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on isolated citation forms (nouns, verbs, possessed forms); no discussion of phrase-level prosody. Data from the Molot village dialect (main Duke of York island). Both documents are unrefereed SIL working drafts ('posted as is without peer review').
new_statements.identity_note: Both Davies & Fritzell documents explicitly describe the Molot village dialect spoken on the main Duke of York island ('This paper describes the Molot dialect of Ramoaaina'); language-level glottocode ramo1244, ISO rai. Vowel symbols in the PDF's legacy font: [ɐ] = orthographic <aa>, [ə] = orthographic <a>.

sources.note: Section 3.1 (pp.3-5): stress is predictable; [ɐ] (orthographic aa) attracts stress, [ə] (orthographic a) repels it, closed syllables attract stress when no [ɐ]; hierarchy (C)V1(C) > (C)V2C > (C)V2 > (C)V3C > (C)V3; stress goes to the strongest syllable, ties to the first; default = first syllable. Secondary stress on every second syllable in both directions from the primary. Tone and length not phonemic (2.3). Exceptions listed ([ˈnəmʲən] 'sweet', [təˈləŋʷən] 'tired', [ˈtəbʷən] 'woman' via ambisyllabic complex consonants; [ˈməge] 'sun').
